procedural_history.originating_court: High Court in its ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction in Suit No. 1623 of 1948.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated June 26, 1952, of the Bombay High Court in Appeal No. 20 of 1952 arising out of the judgment and decree dated December 17, 1951, of the said High Court
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The suit was initially dismissed. The Bombay High Court upheld the dismissal in Appeal No. 20 of 1952.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (originally the plaintiffs) appealed to the Supreme Court after the Bombay High Court upheld the dismissal of their suit. They sought to amend their plaint to include an alternative claim for damages for breach of contract, which was initially denied.

directions: The decree under appeal set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether an amendment of a plaint should be allowed when a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation.

facts: The appellants initially sued the respondents for damages for conversion, alleging an agent-principal relationship.
The suit was dismissed because the court found the relationship was seller-purchaser, and title to the goods had not passed to the appellants, so no conversion occurred.
On appeal to the Supreme Court, the appellants sought to amend their plaint to add an alternative claim for damages for breach of contract for non-delivery of the same goods.
By the time the amendment was requested, a fresh suit for breach of contract would have been barred by the statute of limitations.
The original plaint already contained all the necessary factual allegations to support a claim for breach of contract; it only lacked the specific legal claim in the alternative.
law: As a general rule, courts will decline to allow an amendment if a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation on the date of the application.
However, this is not an absolute rule. The court has the power to allow such an amendment if it is required in the interests of justice.
The fact that the claim is time-barred is a factor to be taken into account in the exercise of the court's discretion, but it does not eliminate the court's power to permit the amendment.
There are cases where special circumstances outweigh the consideration that the amendment would take away a legal right (the defense of limitation) that has accrued to the defendant.
application: The Court acknowledged the strong objection that the amendment would prejudice the defendants by reviving a time-barred claim.
However, the Court found that the "interests of justice" required the amendment in this specific case.
The Court noted that the new claim was not foreign to the scope of the original suit, as both claims arose from the same underlying agreement and transactions.

Crucially, all the factual allegations necessary to sustain the claim for breach of contract were already present in the original plaint. The only thing missing was the formal alternative claim for relief.

The Court also considered the defendants' conduct, suggesting their reason for repudiating the contract was a "mere device" to deprive the plaintiffs of their benefits, which weighed in favor of allowing the amendment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided to allow the amendment. It held that while courts are generally reluctant to permit amendments for claims that are barred by limitation, the power to do so exists and should be exercised when required by the interests of justice. In this case, because all the necessary facts were already pleaded and the new claim was closely related to the original one, justice required that the amendment be granted.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an amendment of a plaint should be allowed when a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation.
appellant_arguments: The appellants (plaintiffs) applied to amend their plaint to add an alternative claim for damages for breach of contract for non-delivery of goods.
The appellants argued that all the necessary factual allegations to sustain this alternative claim were already present in the original plaint.
The appellants contended that the defendants' cancellation of the contract was a mere device to deprive them of benefits, and therefore the justice of the case required the amendment to be granted.
respondent_arguments: The respondents (defendants) resisted the amendment application.
They contended that the amendment introduced a new cause of action.
They argued that a suit on this new cause of action would be barred by the statute of limitations.
They also pointed out that the plaintiffs had ample opportunity to amend their plaint earlier but failed to do so.

cases.principle: An amendment to a plaint should be allowed if the interests of justice require it, even if a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation. The fact that a claim is time-barred is a factor to be considered but does not remove the court's power to allow the amendment.

While a court's power to amend should not as a rule be exercised where it takes away a legal right accrued to a defendant by lapse of time, such considerations can be outweighed by the special circumstances of the case, and the amendment can be allowed if required in the interests of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: While the power to amend a pleading should not as a rule be exercised where it would take away a legal right that has accrued to a defendant by lapse of time, such considerations can be outweighed by the special circumstances of the case. The fact that a claim added by amendment is barred by limitation is a factor to be considered in the exercise of the court's discretion, but it does not affect the court's power to allow the amendment if it is required in the interests of justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that while the fact that a fresh suit on an amended claim would be barred by limitation is a significant factor for a court to consider, it does not affect the court's power to allow the amendment. The court can exercise its discretion to permit such an amendment if it is required in the interests of justice, particularly when the amendment does not introduce a new factual case but merely adds an alternative legal claim based on facts already present in the original plaint.
legal_tests_applied: The rule that courts generally decline to allow amendments if a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation is a factor to be taken into account in the exercise of discretion, not a rule that affects the power of the court to order it if required in the interests of justice.

Citing the Privy Council in Charan Das v. Amir Khan, the court noted that while the power to amend should not as a rule be exercised to take away a legal right accrued by lapse of time, "there are cases where such considerations are out-weighed by the special circumstances of the case."
policy_considerations: The court determined that the "justice of the case" required the amendment to be granted.

The court found that the defendants' ground for repudiating the contract appeared to be a "mere device to deprive the plaintiffs of the benefits of the orders which they had placed," which weighed in favor of allowing the amendment to ensure a fair adjudication on the merits.
